description: Blood clotting begins when injury or inflammation exposes tissue factor to plasma, and this initiation phase produces the first small burst of thrombin that primes the rest of the cascade. Tissue factor (F3) sits on fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and pericytes, normally held in a cryptic, low-activity state; phosphatidylserine exposure and thiol-disulfide rearrangement convert it to its procoagulant form, where it binds factor VII/VIIa with high affinity and the complex cleaves factors IX and X to their active proteases. Cofactors FV and FVIII, von Willebrand factor and prothrombin carry the signal forward, while TFPI, antithrombin and protein S restrain it, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans such as syndecans, glypicans and perlecan provide the surface on which inhibition is accelerated. Unrestrained or ectopic tissue factor activity, including on tumour- and sepsis-derived vesicles, drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation; deficiency of FVIII or FIX causes haemophilia.

When a vessel is injured, platelets not only plug the breach but empty their storage granules into it, and platelet degranulation is that secretory event. The released cargo amplifies platelet recruitment, supports coagulation, and initiates wound repair; loss of granule content or of the machinery that releases it causes bleeding disorders such as gray platelet and storage pool disease. Alpha granules supply adhesive and clotting proteins including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen chains, factor V, thrombospondin and multimerin, along with protease inhibitors of the serpin family and growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF family members that drive angiogenesis and fibrosis. P-selectin and CD63 move to the surface as granule membranes fuse, marking activation. Fusion itself depends on SNARE and regulatory proteins including STXBP2, VTI1B, RAB27B and SYTL4, while integrin alphaIIb-beta3 and the cytoskeletal proteins talin, kindlin-3 and filamin couple activation to secretion.

Raising cytosolic Ca2+ is the switch that converts agonist binding into a functional response in non-excitable cells, and in platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion, integrin activation and aggregation during haemostasis. Two sources are combined. Phospholipase C-generated IP3 opens the ER channels ITPR1-3 to discharge internal stores; the resulting drop in store content is sensed by STIM1, which gathers at ER-plasma membrane contacts and gates the ORAI1/ORAI2 pore to produce store-operated Ca2+ entry that both sustains signalling and refills the store. Independently, ligand- and receptor-operated routes admit Ca2+ directly: the ATP-gated P2X family, with P2X1 prominent in platelets, and TRPC3/6/7 channels. Loss of STIM1 or ORAI1 function produces immunodeficiency and impaired platelet and lymphocyte activation, while excessive entry favours thrombosis, placing this step at the centre of secretion, adhesion and calcium-dependent enzyme control.

Calcium signals must be terminated as sharply as they are generated, and this pathway is how a cell clears calcium from its cytosol after a transient. Pumps of the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum family reload internal stores, plasma membrane calcium ATPases extrude calcium against its gradient using ATP, and sodium/calcium exchangers move it out in exchange for inbound sodium, a lower-affinity but high-capacity route that dominates in cardiac myocytes. Calmodulin senses the rising ion and stimulates the plasma membrane pumps, giving feedback control over the recovery phase; sorcin modulates calcium handling in excitable cells. Restoring resting calcium sets the rate of muscle relaxation, resets neuronal excitability and secretory cells for the next stimulus, and prevents the sustained overload that triggers protease and phospholipase activation and cell death. Failure contributes to heart failure, arrhythmia and hereditary deafness.

Integrins report the state of the extracellular matrix to the cell interior, and this step is how that report reaches the MAP kinase cascade: GRB2 with its exchange factor SOS1 couples an adhesion complex to Ras, converting matrix attachment into proliferative and survival signalling. The context is the activated platelet or adherent cell, where fibrinogen chains, fibronectin and von Willebrand factor engage the ITGA2B/ITGB3 receptor whose cytoplasmic tail is held by talin, with RAP1A/RAP1B and the adaptor APBB1IP acting upstream to bring the receptor into its high-affinity state. Clustering activates focal adhesion kinase (PTK2) and SRC, which phosphorylate sites that recruit the GRB2:SOS pair; loss of this linkage leaves cells attached but unable to translate adhesion into growth-factor-like ERK output, a requirement for anchorage-dependent growth, migration and platelet aggregation.

Thrombin, the protease at the end of the coagulation cascade, also acts as a hormone-like signal by cleaving proteinase-activated receptors on the cell surface, and this route is how a clotting signal becomes a cellular response. In platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion, integrin activation and aggregation, making it central to haemostasis and to arterial thrombosis; the same receptors mediate thrombin's effects on endothelium, smooth muscle and inflammatory cells. Activation is irreversible and unusual: thrombin clips the receptor N-terminus, and the new tethered ligand folds back to activate the receptor, which then couples through Gq and G12/13 heterotrimers to phospholipase C beta, calcium mobilisation, protein kinase C and Rho-dependent cytoskeletal remodelling. Beta-arrestins terminate and redirect signalling, while Src and ERK link receptor activation to growth and differentiation responses. PAR1 is the dominant human thrombin receptor, with PAR4 contributing at higher concentrations.

Healthy vascular endothelium releases prostacyclin continuously, and its action at the Gs-coupled prostacyclin receptor PTGIR keeps platelets quiescent and vessels relaxed. This signalling is the principal brake on spontaneous thrombosis: receptor engagement raises cAMP, activates cAMP-dependent protein kinase, and blocks the rise in cytoplasmic calcium that platelet activation and granule secretion require, while smooth muscle relaxation lowers vascular tone. The genes here are PTGIR together with the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit GNAS and a full complement of beta and gamma subunits that form the heterotrimer transducing receptor occupancy to adenylate cyclase. The output opposes thromboxane A2, the other major eicosanoid arm, and the set point between them governs bleeding versus clotting tendency. Loss of prostacyclin tone contributes to pulmonary arterial hypertension and to the thrombotic risk seen when prostanoid synthesis is pharmacologically shifted.

The contact system feeds into clotting when factor XII autoactivates on a surface: FXIIa converts factor XI to XIa, and plasma kallikrein, generated from prekallikrein bound to high molecular weight kininogen, can also activate factor IX directly, so this FXIIa- and kallikrein-dependent route amplifies fibrin formation while linking coagulation to kinin-driven inflammation. It is not needed for ordinary haemostasis — people lacking factor XII or prekallikrein do not bleed — yet it drives pathological thrombus growth, and factor XII deficiency is associated with protection from venous thrombosis while C1 inhibitor deficiency raises thrombotic risk. That dissociation makes the system an attractive antithrombotic target. Assembly occurs at the platelet surface, where the GPIb-IX-V complex provides a docking platform that concentrates these zymogens; by contrast, factor XI loss does cause bleeding, placing FXI at the junction of the contact and canonical cascades.

Thromboxane A2 is the platelet-derived eicosanoid that drives aggregation and vasoconstriction, and its actions all run through the TP receptor, the target of the antiplatelet drug class that blocks it. Signalling through TP shapes haemostasis, and its overactivity contributes to thrombosis, hypertension and bronchoconstriction, while pharmacological interruption of thromboxane production or receptor engagement is standard cardiovascular prophylaxis. TP exists as two splice variants differing in their cytoplasmic tails, one first described in platelets and placenta and the other in endothelium. Ligand binding couples the receptor to Gq-family alpha subunits, stimulating phospholipase C and raising intracellular calcium to trigger shape change and granule release; coupling to G13 instead activates Rho and Rac for cytoskeletal remodelling. The assortment of beta and gamma subunits here reflects the combinatorial heterotrimers available to this G protein-coupled receptor.

Circulating low-density lipoprotein does not by itself trigger platelets, but at normal plasma concentrations it lowers their threshold for activation, so that thrombin, collagen or ADP produce a larger aggregation response. This sensitization links dyslipidaemia to the prothrombotic tendency seen in atherosclerosis. The apolipoprotein B component of LDL is recognised by ApoER2 (LRP8), a splice variant of the apolipoprotein E receptor family, whose engagement recruits the Src-family kinase Fgr and leads to phosphorylation of p38 MAP kinase on its activation loop. Active p38 phosphorylates cytosolic phospholipase A2, releasing arachidonate for thromboxane production and amplifying granule release and aggregation. The signal is self-limiting: LDL also promotes PECAM-1 signalling, which recruits the phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 together with protein phosphatase 2A holoenzymes to dephosphorylate p38 and terminate the primed state.

Blood vessels need a signal that tells endothelial cells to stay quiescent, stay attached to each other, and survive, and the Tie2 receptor tyrosine kinase encoded by TEK provides it. Angiopoietin-1 and angiopoietin-4 bind and trigger receptor autophosphorylation, while angiopoietin-2 acts largely as a competing ligand that loosens this restraint and primes vessels for sprouting or regression; the balance between them governs vascular stability, permeability, and angiogenic remodelling during development, wound healing, and tumour growth. Phosphorylated Tie2 becomes a docking platform: SHC1, GRB2 with SOS1 and the PTPN11 phosphatase route signals to RAS proteins and the MAP kinase cascade, while p85 regulatory and p110 catalytic PI3K subunits drive AKT-dependent endothelial survival. Loss or mutation of this axis underlies venous malformations, and its dysregulation contributes to sepsis-associated vascular leak and tumour vasculature.

Platelets stick to a damaged vessel wall before they do anything else, and the GPIb-IX-V complex is the receptor that makes that first contact possible. Its four subunits (GP1BA, GP1BB, GP9 and GP5) bind von Willebrand factor immobilised on exposed subendothelial collagen, an interaction that works best under the high shear of arterial flow and tethers a resting platelet long enough for firm adhesion and activation to follow. Loss or defect of the complex causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome, with giant platelets and bleeding; inappropriate engagement at a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque drives the arterial thrombi behind heart attack and stroke. Signalling from the cytoplasmic tail runs through filamin A to the actin cytoskeleton and recruits Src, PI3K regulatory subunit and 14-3-3, while the receptor also docks thrombin for presentation to protease-activated receptors, amplifying activation.

Platelet granule release requires that syntaxin-4 on the plasma membrane be freed from a clamp before it can pair with vesicle SNAREs, and this disinhibition of SNARE formation is the switch that licenses fusion. Munc18-3 (STXBP3) binds syntaxin-4 in a closed conformation that cannot enter a fusion complex; conventional protein kinase C isoforms activated downstream of thrombin, collagen and other platelet agonists phosphorylate the pair and release the constraint, allowing syntaxin-4 to assemble with SNAP and VAMP partners and drive exocytosis of dense granule and alpha granule contents. The result is amplified recruitment and aggregation of platelets at a site of vascular injury, so the step sits at the interface of agonist signal transduction and regulated secretion. Related Munc18-syntaxin control governs insulin granule and immune cell granule release, and defective granule secretion produces bleeding tendency.

Basigin (CD147) is an immunoglobulin-superfamily transmembrane glycoprotein on epithelial and many other cell surfaces that acts both as an adhesion receptor and as an obligatory chaperone for membrane transporters. Its interactions matter because they set the surface level of the monocarboxylate transporters that export lactate from glycolytic cells, and because basigin engagement on neighbouring fibroblasts drives matrix metalloproteinase production and angiogenic VEGF signalling, a combination that supports tumour invasion and metastasis. Partners here include the MCT lactate/pyruvate carriers, the heavy chain 4F2hc with its LAT-family amino acid exchangers, Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunits, caveolin-1, beta1 integrin pairs, and cyclophilin A, which binds the N-terminal Ig-like domain. Homophilic contacts between basigin molecules on apposed cells, plus binding to L1CAM and MAG, link this hub to adhesion, energy metabolism, migration and development.

Platelets stick to exposed collagen at a damaged vessel wall largely through GPVI, and the activation cascade it triggers converts that contact into shape change, granule release and aggregation — the first step of haemostasis and a driver of arterial thrombosis. GPVI pairs with the FcR gamma chain, whose ITAM is phosphorylated by the Src-family kinases Fyn and Lyn, recruiting Syk and assembling a signalosome around the transmembrane adaptor LAT and the cytosolic adaptor SLP-76 (LCP2), much as immune receptors do in T and B cells. Syk output runs through PI3K subunits and PLC-gamma2 to calcium mobilisation and protein kinase C, while VAV exchange factors drive Rac, RhoA and CDC42 for cytoskeletal remodelling; SHP-1 and SHP-2 tune the response. The related receptor CLEC-2, ligated by podoplanin, feeds into the same machinery. Loss of GPVI gives a mild bleeding tendency, and its blockade is pursued as antithrombotic therapy.

When an integrin engages an extracellular matrix ligand, the adhesion it forms must be converted into a growth and motility signal, and this is the branch that carries it to the MAP kinase cascade. Clustering of the platelet integrin αIIbβ3 on fibrinogen, fibronectin or von Willebrand factor, stabilised on the cytoplasmic side by talin and the Rap1 GTPases with their effector RIAM, assembles a focal adhesion kinase–Src complex. Src-dependent phosphorylation of the docking protein p130Cas creates binding sites for the adaptor Crk, and the resulting Cas–Crk module couples adhesion to Ras–ERK activation and to Rac-driven cytoskeletal remodelling. The output is spreading, migration and, in platelets, firm aggregation and clot retraction; loss of the integrin or its activation machinery causes bleeding disorders, while the same signalling axis is exploited by invasive tumour cells.

Once tissue factor has generated a trace of thrombin at a wound, the amplification and propagation phases turn that trace into a burst large enough to clot blood. Thrombin feeds back to activate factors XI, VIII and V on the activated platelet surface, where the tenase complex (FIXa with FVIIIa) makes FXa and the prothrombinase complex (FXa with FVa) cleaves prothrombin, so fibrinogen is converted to cross-linked fibrin and the platelet plug is stabilised. Phosphatidylserine exposure, which requires the scramblase ANO6, and von Willebrand factor binding through the GPIb-IX-V receptor provide the procoagulant membranes and platelet adhesion. Antithrombin, heparin cofactor II and the protein C/protein S system restrain the burst; loss of factor VIII or IX causes haemophilia, while defective inhibition predisposes to thrombosis.

Platelets release ADP from their dense granules when they are activated, and ADP acting back on the P2Y12 receptor is what converts a weak, reversible clump into a stable thrombus. This amplification loop is required for aggregation triggered by every other platelet agonist fcollagen, thrombin, thromboxane, adrenaline, serotonin f and it is the target of the thienopyridine antiplatelet drugs used after coronary stenting; loss-of-function variants cause a bleeding tendency. P2RY12 couples to Gi, so agonist binding releases an inhibitory alpha subunit that lowers adenylate cyclase output and cAMP, relieving protein kinase A restraint on cytoplasmic calcium, while the liberated beta-gamma dimer engages its own effectors. The many G protein alpha, beta and gamma subunits here represent the interchangeable heterotrimer components through which this receptor, and Gi-coupled receptors generally, act. Downstream consequences include granule secretion, thromboxane generation and integrin activation.

cGMP made by guanylate cyclases in response to nitric oxide or natriuretic peptides is the messenger that relaxes smooth muscle, restrains platelets and tunes neuronal excitability, and this pathway covers what happens once it has been made. Its central reader is cGMP-dependent protein kinase, present as the smooth-muscle PRKG1 and the epithelial and neuronal PRKG2, which phosphorylates targets that lower cytosolic calcium: IRAG1 in complex with the IP3 receptor ITPR1 to curb calcium release from internal stores, and large-conductance calcium-activated potassium channels built from KCNMA1 with beta subunits to hyperpolarise the membrane. Signal duration is set by phosphodiesterases that hydrolyse cGMP, among them PDE5A, whose pharmacological inhibition sustains vasodilation and is used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension. Loss of this braking arm favours vasoconstriction and excessive platelet aggregation.

Arachidonic acid, the precursor of prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes, can be liberated not only from phospholipids but also from diacylglycerol, and this route additionally generates the principal endocannabinoid of the nervous system. Diacylglycerol lipases alpha and beta hydrolyse DAG produced by phosphoinositide breakdown – in platelets this DAG is almost entirely arachidonate-bearing – to yield 2-arachidonoylglycerol, an agonist of cannabinoid receptor 1 that mediates retrograde suppression of neurotransmitter release at synapses. Monoacylglycerol lipase, together with the serine hydrolases ABHD6 and ABHD12, then degrades 2-AG to glycerol and free arachidonate, terminating cannabinoid signalling and feeding the eicosanoid pool. The balance between synthesis and hydrolysis sets endocannabinoid tone and links lipid second-messenger signalling to inflammation, pain and neuroprotection; loss of ABHD12 causes a neurodegenerative disorder with ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa.

ADP released from platelet dense granules acts as an autocrine amplifier of haemostasis, and the P2Y1 purinoceptor is the arm of that response that starts shape change and the first, reversible wave of aggregation. It works with the Gi-coupled P2Y12 receptor, the target of clopidogrel and related antithrombotics; both must be engaged for full, irreversible aggregation and thrombus stabilisation, so loss of either leaves a bleeding tendency while excess signalling favours arterial thrombosis. P2Y1 couples to Gq family alpha subunits (GNAQ, GNA11, GNA14, GNA15) with a wide range of beta and gamma partners, mobilising calcium from internal stores. Downstream, p38 MAP kinase and Src-family signalling converge on cytosolic phospholipase A2, releasing arachidonic acid for thromboxane synthesis and recruiting further platelets. The pathway therefore links nucleotide sensing to integrin activation, granule secretion and clot formation.

PECAM-1/CD31 is an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor concentrated at endothelial cell junctions and present on platelets and leukocytes, where its interactions govern leukocyte transendothelial migration, T cell activation, platelet responses and angiogenesis. It engages partners both homophilically, through its extracellular Ig domains, and heterophilically, including with the integrin alphaV/beta3 pair. Its main signalling role is inhibitory: Src-family kinases such as SRC, FYN, LYN, LCK and YES1 phosphorylate tyrosines in the cytoplasmic ITIM motifs, creating docking sites for the SH2-domain phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 and the inositol phosphatase SHIP1, which damp immunoreceptor and integrin signalling and limit PLCgamma-dependent activation. This restraint sets thresholds for platelet aggregation and immune cell activation, while junctional PECAM-1 contributes to endothelial barrier maintenance and mechanosensing of shear stress, linking the receptor to vascular inflammation and thrombosis.

Adrenaline acting on alpha-2 adrenergic receptors is the arm of catecholamine signalling that damps rather than drives cAMP production. The three receptor subtypes encoded here couple preferentially to Gi/Go heterotrimers, so agonist binding inhibits adenylate cyclase and lowers cyclic AMP, while the released G protein subunits also regulate potassium and calcium channels. The physiological consequences are broad: suppression of insulin secretion and promotion of glucagon release from pancreatic islets, contraction of gastrointestinal sphincters, platelet aggregation, and presynaptic autoinhibition of noradrenaline release at sympathetic and central synapses. That last negative feedback loop is why alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine and dexmedetomidine lower sympathetic outflow and blood pressure and produce sedation and analgesia, and why the subtypes differ in their vascular versus neuronal contributions to autonomic tone.

Fibrin formation is the final structural step of blood coagulation, converting soluble plasma fibrinogen into the insoluble meshwork that seals a wounded vessel and gives a clot its mechanical strength. Thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides from the fibrinogen chains, releasing monomers that self-assemble into protofibrils and then thick fibers in a three-dimensional network; activated factor XIII, a transglutaminase, covalently cross-links the fibers in a calcium-dependent manner so the clot resists premature mechanical and enzymatic breakdown. Platelet integrin αIIbβ3 binds the network, linking aggregation to clot retraction and stability. The same module carries the brakes: antithrombin, heparin cofactor II and other serpins neutralize thrombin, while protein C restrains upstream cofactors, so fibrin deposition stays local. Deficiency of fibrinogen or factor XIII causes bleeding and poor wound healing, whereas loss of the inhibitory arm predisposes to thrombosis.
